title: Conditionals
summary: **Conditionals** let your code make decisions — running different branches depending on whether something is true or false. JavaScript gives you if/else if/else, switch, the ternary operator, and logical operators used as control flow, all built on the idea of truthy and falsy values.

subtopics.title: if / else if / else
subtopics.explanation: The if statement runs a block only when its condition is truthy. Add else if to test additional conditions in order, and a final else as a catch-all. The engine checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first matching block, skipping the rest — so order matters when conditions overlap.

subtopics.title: Truthy and falsy in conditions
subtopics.explanation: An if condition doesn't need to be a literal boolean — JavaScript coerces it. The eight falsy values (false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN) take the else path; everything else takes the if path, including '0', [], and {}. Writing if (value) is a common shorthand, but be careful when 0 or '' are valid values you don't want to skip.

subtopics.title: The ternary operator as a conditional
subtopics.explanation: The ternary (condition ? a : b) is a compact, expression-based if/else that returns a value. It's ideal for choosing between two values in an assignment or inside JSX, where statements aren't allowed. Keep ternaries to a single decision — nesting them deeply quickly becomes unreadable and an if/else is clearer.

subtopics.title: switch statements
subtopics.explanation: switch compares one value against multiple case labels using strict equality (===) and runs the matching branch. It's cleaner than a long if/else chain when you're checking the same variable against many discrete values. A default case acts as the fallback when nothing matches.

subtopics.title: Fall-through in switch
subtopics.explanation: Each case runs until it hits a break (or return). Without break, execution 'falls through' into the next case — usually a bug, but intentionally useful for grouping multiple labels that share a body. Always add break unless you specifically want fall-through, and document it when you do.

subtopics.title: Logical operators as control flow
subtopics.explanation: Because && and || short-circuit, they can replace small conditionals. cond && action() runs action only when cond is truthy; value || fallback supplies a default. This is concise for simple cases and is heavily used in React for conditional rendering (isLoggedIn && <Dashboard/>), but a real if is clearer for anything non-trivial.

subtopics.title: Guard clauses (early returns)
subtopics.explanation: A guard clause checks for invalid or edge-case input at the top of a function and returns (or throws) immediately, instead of wrapping the main logic in a big if. This flattens nesting, keeps the 'happy path' un-indented, and makes functions far easier to read. It's a hallmark of clean, professional code.

foundations.overview: Conditionals are how programs branch: they evaluate a condition and choose which code to run. JavaScript offers several forms — if/else if/else for general branching, switch for matching one value against many cases, the ternary for value-returning decisions, and logical operators (&&, ||) for terse control flow. All of them ultimately depend on truthy/falsy coercion.
foundations.formalDefinition: A conditional is a control-flow construct that selects which statements or expressions to execute based on the boolean evaluation of one or more conditions. if/else and switch are statements; the conditional (ternary) operator and logical-operator short-circuiting are expression-based forms of conditional execution.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every meaningful program makes decisions — validating input, choosing UI states, handling errors. Clear conditionals make logic obvious and bug-free; messy ones (deep nesting, missing break, misjudged truthiness) are a top source of beginner bugs and a staple interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a conditional as a fork in the road: the engine evaluates a yes/no question and sends execution down one path. if/else is a chain of forks checked in order; switch is a labeled junction; the ternary is a fork that hands back a value.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine coerces each condition to a boolean (ToBoolean) and jumps to the matching branch, skipping the others. switch compares with strict equality and, without break, simply continues into subsequent cases because there's no implicit boundary between them.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Form validation, feature flags, routing, loading/empty/error UI states, permission checks, and React conditional rendering all run on conditionals — often a mix of if guards, ternaries in JSX, and && short-circuits.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct branching is the difference between a feature that handles every state gracefully and one that crashes or shows the wrong screen; conditional bugs directly produce visible product defects.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Guard clauses and well-structured conditionals keep functions readable and reviewable, while missing break statements and deep nesting create fragile code that's hard to change safely.
foundations.performanceImpact: Branching itself is fast; the practical performance lever is ordering conditions so the cheapest or most common case is checked first, and using switch (or lookup objects) instead of long if/else chains for many discrete values.
commonUseCases: Validating input and handling edge cases with guard clauses
Choosing UI states (loading, empty, error, success)
Mapping a single value to many outcomes with switch
Conditional rendering with && and ternaries in JSX

commonMisconceptions.myth: if conditions must be true/false booleans.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any value works because JavaScript coerces it via truthy/falsy rules, so if (str) or if (arr.length) are valid and common.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Each switch case automatically stops at the next case.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Without break (or return), execution falls through into the following cases, which is a frequent bug.

visualExplorer.title: How an if / else if / else chain is evaluated
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how JavaScript checks conditions in order and runs only the first matching branch.

config.intro: Follow a grading function as it decides which branch to run for a score of 85.

steps.name: Evaluate the first condition
steps.detail: The engine coerces `score >= 90` to a boolean. For 85 this is false, so the first block is skipped.

steps.name: Evaluate the else if
steps.detail: It moves to the next condition `score >= 80`, which is true for 85.

steps.name: Run the matching block
steps.detail: Because this branch matched, its block runs (logs 'B'), and all remaining branches are skipped.

steps.name: Skip the else
steps.detail: Once a branch has matched, the final else is never reached — only one branch ever executes.

steps.name: Continue after the chain
steps.detail: Execution resumes on the line after the whole if/else if/else, having taken exactly one path.

codeLab.title: Refactor nested ifs into guard clauses
codeLab.instructions: Rewrite getDiscount(user) using guard clauses so the happy path isn't deeply nested. Return 0 for a missing user or a missing membership, and return the member discount otherwise. Avoid an else after a return.
hints: Handle the invalid cases first and return early so the rest of the function isn't nested.
After an early return you don't need an else — the happy path can sit un-indented at the end.

debuggingLab.title: The switch that runs too many cases
debuggingLab.symptom: Looking up a role's label returns the wrong string because multiple cases execute.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: There are no break statements, so once 'admin' matches, execution falls through into every following case. Each case overwrites label, so it ends up as 'Viewer' (the last assignment before default). Fall-through continues until a break or the end of the switch.
commonMistakes: Forgetting break, so cases fall through into the next one.
Assuming each case stops automatically at the next case label.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add break statements so each role returns only its own label.

theory.question: What is the difference between if/else and switch, and when would you choose each?
theory.directAnswer: if/else evaluates arbitrary boolean conditions in order and runs the first that's truthy, so it's best for ranges or unrelated conditions. switch compares one value against discrete case labels using strict equality and is cleaner when you're matching the same variable against many fixed values. switch also requires break to avoid fall-through, whereas if/else has no such pitfall.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two branching constructs: if/else for general conditions and switch for value-matching against multiple cases.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: if/else handles any boolean expression; switch is a more readable, sometimes faster form for comparing one value to many discrete options.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: if/else coerces each condition to a boolean and runs the first truthy branch; switch evaluates the expression once, compares it with === against each case, and runs from the matching label until a break or return.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right construct improves readability, and understanding switch's strict-equality matching and fall-through is a common beginner interview check.
theory.realWorldExample: Mapping an HTTP status or a Redux action type to handling logic is clearer with switch; checking score ranges is clearer with if/else if.

nestedTopics.title: Strict equality in switch
nestedTopics.explanation: switch matches cases with ===, so '1' and 1 are different cases.

nestedTopics.title: Fall-through
nestedTopics.explanation: Without break, switch continues into subsequent cases.

nestedTopics.title: Lookup objects
nestedTopics.explanation: An object map is often an even cleaner alternative to switch for value-to-value mapping.

followUps.question: Does switch use == or ===?
followUps.answer: It uses strict equality (===), so there's no type coercion between the switch expression and the case labels.

followUps.question: When would an object map beat a switch?
followUps.answer: When you're purely mapping keys to values; an object lookup is more concise and avoids break-related bugs.

theory.question: What are guard clauses and why are they considered good practice?
theory.directAnswer: A guard clause is an early return (or throw) at the start of a function that handles invalid input or edge cases immediately, before the main logic. It's good practice because it flattens nesting, keeps the main 'happy path' un-indented and readable, and groups all the validation in one obvious place.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An early-exit conditional placed at the top of a function to short-circuit edge cases.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Deeply nested if statements ('arrow code') are hard to read; guard clauses invert the checks to exit early instead.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each guard tests for a disqualifying condition and returns immediately, so by the time execution reaches the bottom, all preconditions are guaranteed and the code can stay flat.

theory.whyImportant: It's a widely-valued readability pattern that interviewers look for, and it prevents the bugs and confusion that come with deep nesting.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler returns early if the user isn't authenticated or required fields are missing, leaving the rest of the function focused on the successful case.

nestedTopics.title: Avoiding else after return
nestedTopics.explanation: Once you return early, the following code is the happy path and needs no else.

nestedTopics.title: Fail fast
nestedTopics.explanation: Validating and exiting early surfaces problems immediately and simplifies later logic.

followUps.question: Why avoid an else after an early return?
followUps.answer: The early return already handles the other case, so an else just adds unnecessary nesting; the happy path can live un-indented at the end.

scenario.question: A function uses if (items) to decide whether to render a list, but it renders even when items is an empty array. Why, and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: An empty array [] is an object, and all objects are truthy, so if (items) is always true regardless of contents. The check should test the length instead — if (items.length > 0) — or, more safely against a missing value, if (items && items.length). The root cause is assuming 'empty' means falsy, which isn't true for arrays.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A truthiness bug where an empty array passes a truthy check it was expected to fail.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: JavaScript's ToBoolean treats all objects (including [] and {}) as truthy; only the eight specific falsy values are false.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Testing items.length asks the real question ('are there any items?'), and combining it with items && guards against null/undefined.

scenario.whyImportant: It's a very common real-world UI bug (empty states rendering wrongly) and tests understanding of truthy/falsy rules.

nestedTopics.title: Objects are truthy
nestedTopics.explanation: [] and {} are truthy because they're objects, not because they're 'empty'.

nestedTopics.title: Safe length check
nestedTopics.explanation: items?.length or items && items.length avoids crashing on null.

followUps.question: Would if (items.length) alone be safe?
followUps.answer: Only if items is guaranteed to exist; if items could be null/undefined, reading .length throws, so guard with items && items.length or items?.length.

coding.question: Write a function categorize(n) that returns 'negative', 'zero', or 'positive' for a number, and 'invalid' for non-numbers — using clear conditionals and a guard clause.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll start with a guard clause for invalid input: if it isn't a finite number, return 'invalid' immediately. That keeps the rest of the function focused on real numbers. Then a simple if/else if/else handles the three numeric cases. I must check for invalid first so NaN doesn't slip into the numeric comparisons.
coding.lineByLine: The first line is a guard clause: anything that isn't a real number (wrong type or NaN) returns 'invalid' and exits early. Because that case is handled, the remaining if checks can safely assume n is a number: less than zero is 'negative', exactly zero is 'zero', and the final return covers all positive values.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a constant number of comparisons.

alternativeApproaches.title: Math.sign with a lookup
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use Math.sign to collapse the numeric branches into a map after the guard clause.

followUps.question: Why check for invalid input before the numeric comparisons?
followUps.answer: Guarding first prevents NaN or wrong types from sneaking through; NaN comparisons are all false, so without the guard a NaN would fall through to 'positive'.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Conditionals structure control flow at every layer — request handlers, state machines, reducers, and UI rendering. Mature codebases favor flat, guard-clause-driven functions and replace sprawling if/else chains or switches with lookup tables and state machines as the number of cases grows.
productionDeepDive.performance: Branching is cheap, but ordering conditions so the most common or cheapest check runs first avoids wasted evaluation, and a switch or object lookup outperforms a long linear if/else chain when matching one value against many options.
productionDeepDive.security: Conditionals enforce authorization and validation; a missing branch, a fall-through bug, or a misjudged truthy check can silently grant access or accept bad input, so explicit, exhaustive conditions matter for safety.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As branching multiplies, teams extract decisions into named predicates, lookup maps, or finite state machines, and use lint rules (no-fallthrough, default-case) to keep large conditional surfaces correct and reviewable.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Guard clauses, exhaustive switch cases with default, and avoiding deep nesting keep logic legible; clever nested ternaries and break-less switches are classic maintenance hazards.
productionDeepDive.observability: Conditional bugs surface as wrong UI states, unexpected branches in logs, or 'impossible' default cases firing; logging which branch was taken and adding a default that records unexpected values helps catch them.

caseStudies.problem: Action handling started as growing if/else chains that were error-prone and hard to extend.
caseStudies.solution: Reducers standardized on switch statements (and later lookup maps) keyed by action type, with a default returning current state.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: switch requires disciplined break/return and a default case, but yields predictable, scalable branching.
caseStudies.lessons: Matching one value against many cases is a job for switch or a lookup map, with a default to handle the unexpected.

Why add a default case to the filter switch?

keyTakeaways: Conditionals branch your code: if/else if/else for general conditions, switch for matching one value against many cases.
Conditions are coerced via truthy/falsy rules, so [] and {} are truthy — check arr.length, not the array itself, for emptiness.
switch matches with strict equality and falls through without break, which is a common bug unless intentional.
The ternary is a value-returning if/else for single decisions; && and || provide concise short-circuit control flow.
Guard clauses (early returns) flatten nesting and keep the happy path readable — a hallmark of clean code.
